extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (students writing math proofs, papers, code, posters, or presentations)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing mathematical writing across short answers, proofs, papers, code, posters, and oral presentations, aimed at undergraduates. Emphasizes clarity, logical flow, appropriate level of detail, formatting, and proper citation/figure practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: State problems carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: State problems carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise and explicit when formulating the problem so readers understand exactly what is being asked or proved. This is listed as a core undergraduate skill in the CUPM Curriculum Guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate [your] assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear any assumptions or hypotheses that underlie your reasoning or model so that conclusions follow transparently from premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value precise definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciate the value of precise definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear definitions for technical terms or notation used; indicate definitions explicitly (e.g., with 'Definition' or typographic emphasis) when they are required within a paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason logically to conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason logically to conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each conclusion follows by logical argument from stated premises and prior results; maintain visible logical flow throughout proofs and derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret results intelligently
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret results intelligently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain what results mean in context, including limitations, significance, and implications for the problem or model under study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read mathematics with understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Read mathematics with understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehend and accurately report prior results and references used in your work; do not misrepresent source material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate with clarity and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate mathematical ideas with clarity and coherence through writing and speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure exposition so that a reader (peer, expert, or lay audience as appropriate) can follow the argument; use clear sentences linking mathematical expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short answer calculations/derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Short answer calculation or derivation requires brief justification, often in phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support short answers with named results when appropriate (e.g., 'l'Hopital's Rule') or well-labeled diagrams that implicitly define variables; brief phrase-level justification is usually sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof structure and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof generally consists of a concise statement of the result followed by 'Proof:' and a well-reasoned argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by stating what is to be shown, label results as Theorem/Lemma/Proposition as appropriate, then provide a logically ordered argument; concise linking sentences are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short paper: exposition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Short papers may involve exposition, results to be proven, external program documentation, or classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific clarifying examples intermixed with general discussion to aid explanation; tailor length and organization to assignment but ensure logical development of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer code documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer code must follow fundamental programming guidelines: meaningful variable names and program documentation are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include comments describing the problem, an overview of the solution, and explanations throughout the code addressing logic and approach; code may appear as calculations, enumerations, simulations, or algorithm implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract composition
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract provides a brief overview, hints at main results, and (if appropriate) includes context indicating importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to venue instructions (minimum/maximum word counts); abstracts are often written early and intentionally broad/concise so they allow readers to decide whether to read/attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer paper structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer papers are often subdivided into sections such as introduction, primary model, critique, future work, and references/acknowledgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduction: give context and necessary background and outline the problem. Primary model: present equations/tables/graphs. Critique: discuss strengths/weaknesses (e.g., complexity vs accuracy). Future work: explore extensions. References: provide complete citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral presentation slide design
rubrics_metrics.description: Slides should organize key information in bulleted lists rather than complete sentences and generally follow a paper's layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First slide: author, affiliation, venue, and date (month and year). Include intro/background, results with supporting output/graphs, conclusions (strengths/weaknesses), acknowledgements, references, and contact info. List software/environment if relevant. Guideline: maximum of six words per line and six lines per slide (except references). Save slides in multiple formats (.pdf) and keep backups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poster design
rubrics_metrics.description: A poster provides an overview and should serve as a stand-alone product as well as a prop for an oral presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to conference-specified dimensions and templates. Compose like a set of slides (title, intro, results, conclusions, references). Include course or project attribution (e.g., 'In partial fulfillment of...'). Use templates carefully and save frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must be substantiated and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics writing, evidence must be substantiated, and evidence must be clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For regressions include the equation and R or R^2; for hypothesis tests include test type, sample size(s), p-value, significance level, and conclusions both in technical terms and in context. Compare multiple fits with appropriate error analysis (e.g., sum of standardized residuals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction and generalization are often the focus; examples are generalized to conjectures or proven statements and code may be abstracted to pseudocode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe processes and rationale so they can be applied to other data or settings; prefer algorithms/pseudocode for generality when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance level of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide enough detail for understanding while avoiding unnecessary laborious detail in the main body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'Where is the math?' to decide if historical/contextual material belongs in the main text or an appendix. Put excessive computational detail or tangential material in appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data reporting and focus on methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: A sample of the data in the body is generally sufficient; focus on methodology rather than rote spreadsheet computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present representative data to illustrate processing; emphasize methods, decisions, and rationale for data handling rather than exhaustive raw output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sources varies by assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of outside sources varies depending on assignment rules (forbidden, optional, or required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow instructor/venue rules. Sources are essential for surveys, historical perspective, or outlining recent advances. When conducting extensive literature review consider annotated bibliographies and separate 'Further Reading' for extraneous sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation style consistency and academic integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single standard citation style; consult instructor or venue and be consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit sources appropriately, report results accurately (do not falsify), prefer paraphrase over direct quotes in math writing, cite data/images created by others, and when in doubt cite. Acknowledge people/institutions (with permission for sensitive info).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs and figures: clarity and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphs and figures should use consistent styles and scales, be clearly labeled, and present only appropriate amounts of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a common numerical scale across related graphs to ease comparison; consider using rates rather than raw counts when appropriate; use logarithmic scales when magnitudes differ greatly and indicate units in captions. Limit to about four to six data sets per graph; use legends; use patterns for B/W reproduction; indicate regression lines (e.g., dashed). Ensure consistent captioning vs titles practice. Number figures/tables/equations consecutively and include captions for each. If a plotted graph uses units like 'hundred thousands' indicate that in the caption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure/table/equation numbering conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbering within a category is generally consecutive; long papers may use section-based numbering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numbering like 'Table 1', 'Figure 1' then 'Table 2', or for long documents 'Table 2.1', 'Table 2.2'. Number equations that are referred to in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence should not begin with a symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix notation with words, but rephrase sentences to start with words (e.g., rewrite 'Let f be a function. f is said to be...' as 'A function f is said to be...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation consistency and reuse rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not recycle symbols in close proximity and do not use two different symbols for the same entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the same symbol 'x' for two different meanings near each other; likewise, don't give one entity multiple symbols. Maintain notation clarity across the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance inline and displayed mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a balance between expressions embedded in text and those displayed on their own lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inline symbols for short expressions and display important equations separately. Include equation numbers when they will be referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice, pronouns, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid contractions, slang, text-speak, or lofty words; use actual nouns rather than ambiguous pronouns like 'they', 'this', or 'it'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, formal academic diction; choose precise nouns instead of vague pronouns to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and tense in mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing in passive voice is common; use present tense for facts and past tense for experiments/methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'I' where reflective writing is appropriate and 'we' occasionally for other contexts. Maintain tense consistency: facts (present), experiments/methods (past).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount vs number usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'amount' for continuous quantities and 'number' for discrete counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply correct word choice for precision (e.g., 'amount of biomass' vs 'number of apples').

rubrics_metrics.name: Document formatting: spacing, headers, and draft labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts are generally single-spaced; longer papers double-spaced. Multi-page writing benefits from header/footer and page numbers; include draft/version info when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Header often includes author's last name and title; footer contains page number. First page typically not numbered. Include date or draft number for iterative submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and drafting practical tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious when copying content across software; use consistent formatting and control graphics carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dashes for numeric bulleted lists to prevent negative-looking items; maintain consistent bullet formatting; when pasting images into Word leave blank lines before/after or paste into a table cell; save images in same folder as LaTeX file; learn LaTeX for ongoing mathematical work; Google Docs is convenient for collaboration but has fewer formatting features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing workflow and backups
rubrics_metrics.description: During drafting focus on wording first and mark placeholders for figures; keep multiple named versions and back up files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear file names (e.g., Course_LastName_version), maintain multiple copies (Google Drive, campus server, USB), and save slides in multiple formats including .pdf to prevent loss and allow portability.
